course: Small Kiosk and Tuck Shop Business

lessons.title: Setting Up a Simple Inventory System
lessons.body: Start with a notebook and pen. That's your inventory system. Don't wait for a computer or smartphone. In your notebook, create a table with columns: Date, Item, Quantity In, Quantity Out, Balance. Every time you buy stock, write it in. Every time you sell, write it out. At the end of the day, calculate the balance. For example, if you start with 50 loaves of bread, sell 30, your balance is 20. This simple method works. If you have a smartphone, use a free app like Inventory Management or Zoho Inventory. But the notebook is reliable and doesn't need electricity. Number your pages and keep a separate page for each major category: drinks, snacks, household items. Use a ruler to draw lines. Keep your notebook in a safe place, not on the counter where customers can see. At the end of each week, total your sales and compare with your stock counts. This helps you spot mistakes early. Remember, the goal is to know what you have and what you've sold. Even a simple system is better than none. Start today with what you have.

lessons.title: Tracking Stock Levels and Reorder Points
lessons.body: A reorder point is the number of items left when you must order more. If you sell 10 bottles of soda per day and it takes 2 days for your supplier to deliver, you need at least 20 bottles as a buffer. So your reorder point is 20. When your stock hits 20, you order. To track stock levels, count your items every morning before opening. Write the count in your notebook. During the day, record each sale. At closing, count again. The difference is your sales. If you sell 10 sodas, your stock should drop by 10. If it drops by 15, you have a problem: theft, breakage, or a recording error. For fast-moving items like airtime or sweets, check twice a day. For slow items like washing powder, check weekly. Use a simple formula: Reorder Point = (Average Daily Sales x Lead Time) + Safety Stock. Safety stock is extra to cover unexpected demand. For a kiosk, keep safety stock of 20-30% of your daily sales. For example, if you sell 20 loaves a day and lead time is 1 day, reorder point = 20 + 6 = 26. So when you have 26 loaves left, order more. Adjust as you learn your customers' habits.

lessons.title: Preventing Theft and Shrinkage
lessons.body: Shrinkage is lost stock from theft, damage, or errors. In a kiosk, common causes are customers stealing, employees stealing, and supplier short-delivery. To prevent customer theft, keep small expensive items like phone chargers behind the counter. Use a mirror to see blind spots. Greet every customer and make eye contact. For employee theft, never let one person handle both stock and cash. If you have workers, rotate duties. Count stock before and after each shift. Use a cash register or a locked box for money. Never leave money unattended. For supplier theft, count every delivery in front of the driver. Check the invoice against what you ordered. If items are missing, note it on the delivery note and call the supplier immediately. Also, watch for damage: keep perishables cool, stack boxes properly. Breakage is shrinkage too. Keep a shrinkage log: date, item, quantity lost, reason. Review it weekly. If you see a pattern, fix it. For example, if you lose 5 chocolates every week, move them closer to you. Shrinkage of 2% of sales is normal; above 5% is a crisis. Train your workers on these rules. Offer a small bonus for zero shrinkage. It works.

lessons.title: Managing Perishable Goods
lessons.body: Perishables like milk, bread, fruits, and vegetables spoil quickly. Order small quantities more often. For bread, order daily. For milk, order every two days. Check expiry dates when you receive stock. Sell older items first: put new stock behind old stock. Use a first-in, first-out (FIFO) system. For fruits and vegetables, inspect daily. Remove spoiled ones immediately so they don't spread rot. If you have a fridge, keep it at 4Â°C for milk and 0Â°C for meat. Without a fridge, use a cooler box with ice. Sell perishables at a discount near closing time to avoid total loss. For example, if you have 10 loaves left at 6 PM, sell them at half price. You lose some profit but recover your cost. Keep a record of spoilage: date, item, quantity, reason. If you spoil 5 loaves a week, reduce your daily order by 5. In hot climates, perishables spoil faster. Buy from local farmers who harvest daily. Consider partnering with a nearby restaurant to sell your near-expiry items at a discount. Never sell spoiled food; it harms your reputation and can make people sick. Health first, profit second.

lessons.title: Conducting Regular Stock Audits
lessons.body: A stock audit is a physical count of everything you have. Do it at least once a week, preferably on a slow day. Close the kiosk or do it after hours. Count every item: tins, bottles, packets. Write the counts in your notebook. Compare with your inventory records. The difference is your shrinkage or error. For example, if your records show 100 sweets but you count 92, you have a shortage of 8. Investigate: was it theft, breakage, or a recording mistake? Check your sales records. If you sold 50 and started with 150, you should have 100. If you have 92, something is wrong. Do a full audit monthly. Use a checklist to ensure you don't miss items. Count shelves from top to bottom, left to right. Have someone else count too, if possible, to avoid bias. After the audit, update your records. Adjust your reorder points if needed. If you find a consistent shortage in one item, take action: move it, secure it, or stop selling it. Audits help you know your true profit. Without them, you might think you're making money when you're actually losing stock. Keep audit sheets for at least 6 months. They help you spot trends and plan better.

lessons.title: Using Inventory Data to Make Decisions
lessons.body: Your inventory data tells you what to buy, what to drop, and when to run promotions. Look at your sales records. Which items sell fastest? Stock more of those. Which items sit for weeks? Stop ordering them or reduce quantity. For example, if you sell 50 bottles of water daily but only 2 cans of beans, focus on water. Calculate your profit per item: selling price minus cost. If an item has low profit and slow sales, drop it. Use data to negotiate with suppliers. If you buy 100 loaves a week, ask for a discount. If you buy in bulk, you save money. But don't overstock perishables. Use data to set reorder points accurately. If sales increase during holidays, adjust your orders. Track seasonal trends: more cold drinks in hot months, more snacks during school terms. Use a simple spreadsheet or notebook to calculate your turnover rate: how many times you sell and replace stock in a month. High turnover means good cash flow. Low turnover means dead stock. Also, calculate your gross margin: (sales - cost of goods sold) / sales. Aim for at least 20% for a kiosk. If it's lower, raise prices or find cheaper suppliers. Review your data weekly and make one change at a time. Small adjustments lead to big profits.

quiz.q: What is the simplest tool to start an inventory system?
quiz.explanation: A notebook and pen are the simplest and most reliable tools, requiring no electricity or technical skills.

quiz.q: How often should you record stock in and out in your inventory notebook?
options: B) Every time you buy or sell
quiz.explanation: Recording every transaction keeps your inventory accurate and helps spot discrepancies early.

quiz.q: What is a reorder point?
options: A) The number of items left when you must order more
B) The price at which you reorder
C) The time of day you order
quiz.explanation: A reorder point is the stock level that triggers a new order to avoid running out.

quiz.q: If you sell 10 sodas per day and it takes 2 days for delivery, what is your minimum reorder point without safety stock?
quiz.explanation: You need 10 sodas per day for 2 days, so 10 x 2 = 20 sodas as reorder point.

quiz.q: What is safety stock?
options: A) Extra stock to cover unexpected demand
B) Stock kept in a safe
quiz.explanation: Safety stock is a buffer to prevent stockouts when demand is higher than expected or delivery is delayed.

quiz.q: How often should you count fast-moving items like airtime?
quiz.explanation: Fast-moving items need frequent checks to catch theft or errors quickly.

quiz.q: What is shrinkage?
options: A) Loss of stock from theft, damage, or errors
quiz.explanation: Shrinkage refers to the difference between recorded inventory and actual inventory, often due to loss.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common cause of shrinkage in a kiosk?
quiz.explanation: All three are common causes of shrinkage in small retail businesses.

quiz.q: What is a good practice to prevent employee theft?
options: A) Let one person handle both stock and cash
B) Rotate duties and count stock before and after shifts
quiz.explanation: Rotating duties and regular counts reduce opportunities for theft and make it easier to detect.

quiz.q: What should you do if a supplier delivers fewer items than ordered?
options: B) Note it on the delivery note and call the supplier
quiz.explanation: Documenting the shortage and informing the supplier immediately helps resolve the issue and prevents future losses.

quiz.q: What is a normal shrinkage rate for a small kiosk?
quiz.explanation: A shrinkage rate of about 2% is considered normal; above 5% is a serious problem.

quiz.q: Why should you keep small expensive items behind the counter?
options: B) To make them look better
D) To hide them from customers
quiz.explanation: Keeping high-value items out of easy reach reduces the risk of theft.

quiz.q: What does FIFO stand for in inventory management?
quiz.explanation: FIFO means selling older stock first to reduce spoilage and expiry losses.

quiz.q: How should you store perishable goods like milk without a fridge?
options: A) In a cooler box with ice
quiz.explanation: A cooler box with ice helps keep perishables cool and extends their shelf life.

quiz.q: What should you do with near-expiry perishables?
quiz.explanation: Discounting near-expiry items recovers some cost and prevents total loss.

quiz.q: How often should you conduct a full stock audit?
quiz.explanation: A monthly full audit helps you detect and address inventory issues regularly.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a stock audit?
options: A) To count physical stock and compare with records
quiz.explanation: A stock audit verifies actual inventory against records to identify discrepancies.

quiz.q: If your records show 100 sweets but you count 92, what does this indicate?
quiz.explanation: A shortage means you have fewer items than recorded, indicating loss or error.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep audit sheets for at least 6 months?
options: A) To spot trends and plan better
B) To use as toilet paper
quiz.explanation: Historical audit data helps identify patterns and make informed decisions.

quiz.q: What does inventory data help you decide?
options: A) What to buy, what to drop, and when to promote
D) Where to go on holiday
quiz.explanation: Inventory data informs purchasing, discontinuing, and promotional decisions.

quiz.q: If an item has low profit and slow sales, what should you do?
options: A) Drop it or reduce order quantity
quiz.explanation: Low-profit, slow-moving items tie up capital and shelf space; it's better to replace them.

quiz.q: How can you use inventory data to negotiate with suppliers?
options: A) Show them your bulk purchase volume and ask for a discount
quiz.explanation: Demonstrating consistent bulk purchases gives you leverage to negotiate better prices.

quiz.q: What is turnover rate?
options: A) How many times you sell and replace stock in a period
B) How fast you turn around in the shop
C) The number of customers per day
D) The speed of your delivery
quiz.explanation: Turnover rate measures how quickly inventory is sold and replenished, indicating cash flow efficiency.

quiz.q: What is a good gross margin target for a kiosk?
quiz.explanation: A 20% gross margin is a common benchmark for small retail to cover costs and profit.

quiz.q: How often should you review your inventory data to make decisions?
quiz.explanation: Weekly reviews allow you to make timely adjustments and stay on top of trends.

quiz.q: What is the first step in setting up a simple inventory system?
options: A) Buy a notebook and pen
quiz.explanation: Starting with basic tools like a notebook and pen is the simplest and most accessible first step.

quiz.q: Why is it important to record sales immediately?
options: A) To keep accurate inventory records
quiz.explanation: Immediate recording ensures inventory data is up-to-date and reduces errors.

quiz.q: What should you do if you notice a consistent shortage in one item?
options: A) Move it, secure it, or stop selling it
quiz.explanation: Addressing the root cause of a consistent shortage prevents further losses.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of using a first-in, first-out (FIFO) system for perishables?
options: A) It reduces spoilage by selling older stock first
quiz.explanation: FIFO ensures older items are sold before they expire, minimizing waste.

quiz.q: What should you do with spoiled perishables?
options: A) Remove them immediately and record the loss
B) Sell them at a discount
C) Mix them with fresh ones
quiz.explanation: Removing spoiled items prevents contamination and recording the loss helps track shrinkage.
